The existence of the compatible lattice order on the complex field ℂ\mathbb{C}

Zhengmao He Address: School of Sciences, Southwest Petroleum University,Chengdu 610500,Sichuan China
Abstract

In this paper, we give an affirmative answer to the open question posed by G. Birkhoff and R. S. Pierce in 1956 concerning the existence of a compatible lattice order on the complex field ℂ\mathbb{C}. Using valuation rings theory, basis extension in infinite-dimensional vector spaces and extension of field embeddings to algebraic extensions, we obtain that for every real t>1t>1 transcendental over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the compatible lattice order can be chosen such that 0≺10\prec 1, 0∨i=t0\vee i=t, and 1∧t=01\wedge t=0. Consequently, ℂ\mathbb{C} admits at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}} distinct compatible lattice orders, each extending the usual order on ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Keywords: 
compatible lattice order; complex field ℂ\mathbb{C}; valuation rings theory; field embedding; infinite-dimensional vector space
Mathematics Subject Classification: 06F25; 12J15; 12J20

1 Introduction

The interaction between order and multiplication is a central theme in the theory of ordered algebraic structures. A partial order ⪯\preceq on a field LL is compatible with its ring operations if translation preserves order and the product of two nonnegative elements is nonnegative. Thus x⪯yx\preceq y implies x+a⪯y+ax+a\preceq y+a, and 0⪯x0\preceq x, 0⪯y0\preceq y imply 0⪯x​y0\preceq xy. Such an order is a lattice order if every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound, denoted by x∨yx\vee y and x∧yx\wedge y. Throughout this paper, a lattice-ordered field means a field equipped with these ring-order and lattice properties. The order need not be total, and positivity of inverses is not included as an additional axiom.

The familiar obstruction to ordering ℂ\mathbb{C} concerns total field orders. In a totally ordered field every nonzero square is positive, which is incompatible with i2=−1i^{2}=-1. For a partial order, however, an element may be incomparable with zero, so this argument does not exclude a compatible lattice order. Conversely, the coordinate order has joins and meets but is incompatible with multiplication: it makes ii nonnegative while i2=−1i^{2}=-1 is negative. These two observations identify the difficulty. One must construct enough order structure to obtain least and greatest bounds while retaining multiplicative closure of the positive cone.

In their 1956 paper on lattice-ordered rings, G. Birkhoff and R. S. Pierce posed the question whether the complex field admits a lattice order compatible with its ring operations [2]. This question, usually called the Birkhoff–Pierce problem for the complex field, belongs to a broader programme concerning partial orders on familiar fields and division rings. In 1963, Fuchs formulated the related Problem 31, asking for a description of the directed orders on the complex and quaternion fields [5, p. 212]. Directedness requires common upper and lower bounds, whereas a lattice order requires least upper and greatest lower bounds. Every lattice order is directed, but the converse fails; maintaining this distinction is essential when comparing the subsequent existence results.

An important early development concerned the real field. Wilson constructed non-total lattice orders on subfields of ℝ\mathbb{R} and proved that ℝ\mathbb{R} admits 2𝔠2^{\mathfrak{c}} distinct lattice orders, where 𝔠=2ℵ0\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_{0}} is the cardinality of the continuum [11]. Thus the usual total order does not exhaust the lattice orders compatible with real-field arithmetic. This result established considerable flexibility on the real side, but it did not supply an order on ℂ\mathbb{C}, where the presence of ii prevents the use of total-order arguments. Schwartz subsequently investigated the structure of lattice-ordered fields, particularly their relation to totally ordered subfields and to algebraic extensions [8]. As recalled by Schwartz and Yang [7], this work also gives an obstruction in the algebraic-number setting: a number field admitting a compatible lattice order must be real.

The directed version of the existence problem developed further through constructions allowing negative squares. Yang proved the existence of directed rings and algebras with this feature [12]. Schwartz and Yang then established the existence of compatible directed partial orders on 𝒞\mathcal{C} [9]. Their later characterization states that a field admits a compatible directed partial order precisely when it has characteristic zero and is either formally real or has positive transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q} [7, Theorem 4]. In particular, transcendence permits directed orders on fields that cannot be totally ordered. This criterion settles the directed existence question, but it does not provide joins and meets.

Other work has studied partial orders on quadratic extensions and quaternion algebras while keeping a specified ordered coefficient domain fixed; see, for example, Ma [6]. More recently, Wang, Yuan, Zhang, and Zhu constructed explicit directed positive cones on ℂ\mathbb{C} using integral closures of local rings [10]. Their nonzero positive elements are closed under inversion. They proved that none of the orders in that family is a lattice order, since 00 and ii have no least upper bound. Their September 2026 preprint accordingly still records the general lattice-order problem as open and conjectures a negative answer. The failure of joins for those cones is a statement about that construction, rather than a general obstruction to all compatible partial orders on ℂ\mathbb{C}.

In the present paper, we give an affirmative answer to the Birkhoff–Pierce problem. We construct lattice orders on the usual complex field and prescribe specific lattice identities involving the original complex numbers 11, ii, and a chosen transcendental real parameter. More precisely, our principal result is the following.

Theorem 1.1.

For every real number t>1t>1 transcendental over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, there exists a partial order ⪯\preceq on the usual field ℂ\mathbb{C} that is compatible with addition and multiplication and makes ℂ\mathbb{C} a lattice. Its restriction to ℚ\mathbb{Q} is the usual order, and it satisfies 0≺10\prec 1, 0∨i=t0\vee i=t, and 1∧t=01\wedge t=0. Moreover, the construction preserves the order and the binary lattice operations on a specified countable algebraically closed subfield containing ℚ⁡(t,i)\mathbb{Q}(t,i).

Here x≺yx\prec y means x⪯yx\preceq y and x≠yx\neq y. Since the value of 0∨i0\vee i is determined by the order relation, distinct parameters tt produce distinct compatible lattice orders. There are 𝔠\mathfrak{c} real transcendental numbers greater than 11, so ℂ\mathbb{C} admits at least 𝔠\mathfrak{c} distinct such orders. This is a lower bound for distinct order relations on the fixed complex field; no classification up to field automorphism is asserted.

Our approach separates the construction into a countable algebraic stage and a passage to the full complex field. Fix the parameter tt and put F=ℚ⁡(t)F=\mathbb{Q}(t). Let KK be the set of elements of ℂ\mathbb{C} algebraic over FF. Then KK is countable and algebraically closed. Countability makes it possible to enumerate all its elements and to satisfy their spanning requirements one at a time. At this stage the objective is stronger than the construction of a directed cone: we seek a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-basis BB of KK for which every product of basis elements is a finite nonnegative rational linear combination of basis elements.

Such a basis immediately gives a lattice order. Its nonnegative coordinate cone PBP_{B} defines x≤Kyx\leq_{K}y by y−x∈PBy-x\in P_{B}, and the join and meet are obtained by taking coordinatewise maxima and minima. Multiplicative compatibility is equivalent to the required nonnegativity of the multiplication coefficients on basis products. An arbitrary basis offers no reason for those coefficients to be nonnegative. The main constructive issue is therefore to enlarge a basis while imposing finitely many positivity requirements and preserving all coordinate calculations already made.

We resolve this issue by a finite basis-extension lemma. Suppose an existing basis spans a subspace VV, and a finite set of new targets lies in an affine hyperplane on which a rational linear functional has value 11, while the functional vanishes on VV. A suitable change of the new basis vectors, together with a common correction in the old nonnegative cone, places all targets in the enlarged nonnegative cone. The enlarged basis contains the original basis, and the new cone intersects VV in exactly the old cone. This finite-dimensional calculation is the mechanism that preserves earlier stages. Its affine normalization also explains the role of valuation theory in the argument.

On FF, the degree of a nonzero rational function is deg⁡p−deg⁡q\deg p-\deg q for p⁡(t)q⁡(t)\frac{p(t)}{q(t)} with nonzero p,q∈ℚ⁡[x]p,q\in\mathbb{Q}[x]. The negative of this function is the valuation at infinity. Extending it to the algebraic field KK gives a rational-valued degree function δ\delta, with δ⁡(t)=1\delta(t)=1, δ⁡(q)=0\delta(q)=0 for q∈ℚ×q\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}, δ⁡(x​y)=δ⁡(x)+δ⁡(y)\delta(xy)=\delta(x)+\delta(y), and δ⁡(x+y)≤max⁡{δ⁡(x),δ⁡(y)}\delta(x+y)\leq\max\{\delta(x),\delta(y)\}. Standard valuation-extension results and the torsion property of value-group extensions in algebraic field extensions explain why the values can be normalized in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}; see Engler and Prestel [3]. We also give the requisite construction through a dominating valuation ring.

Write 𝒪={x∈K:δ⁡(x)≤0}\mathcal{O}=\{x\in K:\delta(x)\leq 0\} and m={x∈K:δ⁡(x)<0}m=\{x\in K:\delta(x)<0\}, with δ⁡(0)=−∞\delta(0)=-\infty. The residue field k=𝒪/mk=\mathcal{O}/m contains a canonical copy of ℚ\mathbb{Q}. For each nonnegative integer nn, the subspace Kn={x∈K:δ⁡(x)≤n}K_{n}=\{x\in K:\delta(x)\leq n\} carries a linear map ℓn​(x)=res⁡(x/tn)\ell_{n}(x)=\operatorname{res}(x/t^{n}) into kk. This map vanishes exactly on the elements of degree less than nn and satisfies ℓn​(tn)=1\ell_{n}(t^{n})=1. Furthermore, the maps respect multiplication across the filtration: ℓr+s​(x​y)=ℓr​(x)​ℓs​(y)\ell_{r+s}(xy)=\ell_{r}(x)\ell_{s}(y) when x∈Krx\in K_{r} and y∈Ksy\in K_{s}. These properties allow products and spanning targets to be normalized by the same functional.

The inductive construction produces finite layers BnB_{n}, starting with B0={1}B_{0}=\{1\} and B1={t,t−i}B_{1}=\{t,t-i\}, such that δ⁡(b)=n\delta(b)=n and ℓn​(b)=1\ell_{n}(b)=1 for b∈Bnb\in B_{n}. At stage nn, we impose positivity on tnt^{n} and on the products b​cbc with b∈Brb\in B_{r}, c∈Bsc\in B_{s}, r,s≥1r,s\geq 1, and r+s=nr+s=n. Both factors then belong to earlier stages, so these product requirements introduce no circular dependence. To ensure that the final basis spans KK, choose an enumeration K={x1,x2,…}K=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots\} and strictly increasing positive integers Nj>δ⁡(xj)N_{j}>\delta(x_{j}). At stage NjN_{j}, include the additional target tNj−xjt^{N_{j}}-x_{j}. Once both this target and tNjt^{N_{j}} belong to the constructed span, so does xjx_{j}.

Every target at stage nn has ℓn\ell_{n}-value 11, while every element of the old span has ℓn\ell_{n}-value zero. Although kk need not equal ℚ\mathbb{Q}, the restriction of ℓn\ell_{n} to the space generated by the old span and these targets takes values in the canonical copy of ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The finite basis-extension lemma therefore applies over precisely the required scalar field. At the limit, every element of KK has entered the span and every product of basis elements has entered the nonnegative cone. The union B=⋃n≥0BnB=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}B_{n} is consequently a positive basis with the desired multiplication property. The initial choice of B1B_{1} yields i=t−(t−i)i=t-(t-i), and the coordinate lattice formulas give 0∨Ki=t0\vee_{K}i=t and 1∧Kt=01\wedge_{K}t=0.

It remains to obtain an order on all of ℂ\mathbb{C}. Rather than carry out the same finite scheduling directly through an uncountable construction, we pass to the ultrapower E=Kℕ/𝒰E=K^{\mathds{N}}/\mathcal{U} for a nonprincipal ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} on ℕ\mathbb{N}. This step preserves the field operations, the order relation, and the binary lattice operations simultaneously. The usual preservation principle for ultraproducts provides the general model-theoretic background [13]; here the required properties are verified directly on representatives. In particular, EE is algebraically closed of characteristic zero, and the diagonal embedding j:K⟶Ej:K\longrightarrow E preserves and reflects order and preserves joins and meets.

The cardinality calculation is equally important. Countability of KK gives |E|≤𝔠|E|\leq\mathfrak{c}, and a coding of binary sequences by their finite initial segments gives the reverse inequality. Thus |E|=𝔠|E|=\mathfrak{c}. Since KK is countable, both EE and ℂ\mathbb{C} have transcendence degree 𝔠\mathfrak{c} over their respective copies of KK. Matching transcendence bases gives an isomorphism of the corresponding rational function fields. An embedding-extension argument for algebraic extensions then produces a field embedding Φ:E⟶ℂ\Phi:E\longrightarrow\mathbb{C} satisfying Φ⁡(j⁡(a))=a\Phi(j(a))=a for every a∈Ka\in K. Its image is algebraically closed, and ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraic over that image, so Φ\Phi is surjective.

Finally, transport the lattice order of EE through Φ\Phi. Because Φ\Phi is a field isomorphism, the transported order is compatible with the original addition and multiplication on 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Because Φ\Phi fixes the diagonal copy of KK, the prescribed identities for the actual numbers tt and ii survive the transport. Fixing KK is therefore essential: an unspecified abstract isomorphism would not by itself ensure those identities for the chosen complex numbers. The proof combines valuation rings, finite extensions of bases in infinite-dimensional rational vector spaces, nonprincipal ultrafilters, transcendence bases, and extension of field embeddings.

The scope of the resulting order is reflected in its prescribed identities. Since t>1t>1 in the ordinary real order but 1∧t=01\wedge t=0 in our lattice, the order does not extend the usual order on all of ℝ\mathbb{R}. It does extend the usual rational order. Also, tt is positive whereas neither t−1t^{-1} nor −t−1-t^{-1} is nonnegative. On the countable field this follows from the fact that every nonzero element of PBP_{B} has nonnegative integral degree, while δ⁡(t−1)=−1\delta(t^{-1})=-1, and it remains true after transport. Thus closure under inversion is absent, distinguishing the construction from the inversion-closed directed cones discussed above. The argument is algebraic and uses choice through maximality arguments and the ultrafilter construction.

The paper develops these ingredients in the order required by the proof. We first establish the finite positive basis-extension principle and the valuation and residue calculations. We then construct the countable positive basis and describe its coordinate lattice order, including the initial layers and the degree restrictions on positive elements. The ultrapower construction and the field isomorphism fixing KK provide the passage to ℂ\mathbb{C}. The final results give the main theorem and explicit formulas for comparisons, joins, and meets in terms of representatives and rational basis coordinates.

2 Preliminaries

We collect the terminology and algebraic tools used in the construction. All rings are commutative with identity, all subrings contain the ambient identity, and all field embeddings preserve it. We write ℕ0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\} and 𝔠=2ℵ0\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_{0}}.

2.1 Positive cones and compatible lattice orders

A positive cone in a field LL is a subset PP such that 0∈P0\in P, P+P⊆PP+P\subseteq P, P​P⊆PPP\subseteq P, and P∩(−P)={0}P\cap(-P)=\{0\}. It defines a partial order by x≤yx\leq y if and only if y−x∈Py-x\in P. This order is translation invariant, and products of nonnegative elements are nonnegative. We call it a compatible lattice order if every pair has a least upper bound x∨yx\vee y and a greatest lower bound x∧yx\wedge y. A directed order requires only common upper and lower bounds. Lattice orders are directed; they need not be total, and positivity of inverses is not assumed. These conventions concern lattice-ordered rings whose underlying rings are fields [5].

2.2 Rational bases and finite positive extensions

A ℚ\mathbb{Q}-basis BB of a vector space VV is a Hamel basis: every x∈Vx\in V has a unique expansion x=∑b∈Bxb​bx=\sum_{b\in B}x_{b}b, with xb∈ℚx_{b}\in\mathbb{Q} and finite support. Its coordinate cone is PB={∑b∈Bqbb:qb∈ℚ≥0,finite support}P_{B}=\{\sum_{b\in B}q_{b}b:q_{b}\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0},\ \text{finite support}\}. Then x≤Byx\leq_{B}y is equivalent to xb≤ybx_{b}\leq y_{b} for every b∈Bb\in B. The lattice operations are x∨By=∑bmax{xb,yb}bx\vee_{B}y=\sum_{b}\max\{x_{b},y_{b}\}b and x∧By=∑bmin{xb,yb}bx\wedge_{B}y=\sum_{b}\min\{x_{b},y_{b}\}b. Both sums have support contained in the union of the supports of xx and yy.

If 1∈B1\in B, the order on ℚ\mathbb{Q} is the usual one. When VV is a field, the condition b​c∈PBbc\in P_{B} for all b,c∈Bb,c\in B guarantees PB​PB⊆PBP_{B}P_{B}\subseteq P_{B} by distributivity. The finite extension lemma proved in our construction asserts the following. If BB is a basis of VV, AA is a nonempty finite subset of a larger rational vector space, W=V+spanℚ⁡AW=V+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{Q}}A, and a rational linear map λ:W→ℚ\lambda:W\to\mathbb{Q} satisfies λ⁡(V)=0\lambda(V)=0 and λ⁡(a)=1\lambda(a)=1 for a∈Aa\in A, then a finite set B′B^{\prime} can be chosen so that B∪B′B\cup B^{\prime} is a basis of WW, λ⁡(b′)=1\lambda(b^{\prime})=1 for b′∈B′b^{\prime}\in B^{\prime}, A⊆PB∪B′A\subseteq P_{B\cup B^{\prime}}, and PB∪B′∩V=PBP_{B\cup B^{\prime}}\cap V=P_{B}. Thus finitely many positivity requirements can be imposed without altering the old coordinates.

2.3 Local rings, valuation rings, and residue maps

A local ring (R,𝔪R)(R,\mathfrak{m}_{R}) has a unique maximal ideal; equivalently, its nonunits form the ideal 𝔪R\mathfrak{m}_{R}. A module MM is finitely generated if M=R​u1+⋯+R​urM=Ru_{1}+\cdots+Ru_{r} for finitely many elements uju_{j}. Nakayama’s lemma states that 𝔪R​M=M\mathfrak{m}_{R}M=M then implies M=0M=0. A local subring (S,𝔫)(S,\mathfrak{n}) of a field dominates (R,𝔪R)(R,\mathfrak{m}_{R}) if R⊆SR\subseteq S and 𝔫∩R=𝔪R\mathfrak{n}\cap R=\mathfrak{m}_{R}. Every local subring of a field is dominated by a valuation ring in that field. A valuation ring 𝒪\mathcal{O} of LL is characterized by the property that x∈𝒪x\in\mathcal{O} or x−1∈𝒪x^{-1}\in\mathcal{O} for every x∈L×x\in L^{\times}.

A rational-valued valuation ν:L×→ℚ\nu:L^{\times}\to\mathbb{Q} is additive on products and satisfies ν⁡(x+y)≥min⁡{ν⁡(x),ν⁡(y)}\nu(x+y)\geq\min\{\nu(x),\nu(y)\} when x+y≠0x+y\neq 0; set ν⁡(0)=+∞\nu(0)=+\infty. For the present application, fix a real transcendental t>1t>1, put F=ℚ⁡(t)F=\mathbb{Q}(t), and let K⊆ℂK\subseteq\mathbb{C} consist of the elements algebraic over FF. The field KK is countable and algebraically closed. The valuation at infinity on FF, given by ν0​(p⁡(t)/q⁡(t))=deg⁡q−deg⁡p\nu_{0}(p(t)/q(t))=\deg q-\deg p for nonzero p,q∈ℚ⁡[X]p,q\in\mathbb{Q}[X], extends to a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-valued valuation ν\nu on KK [3]. Set δ=−ν\delta=-\nu and δ⁡(0)=−∞\delta(0)=-\infty. Then δ⁡(x​y)=δ⁡(x)+δ⁡(y)\delta(xy)=\delta(x)+\delta(y) for nonzero x,yx,y, and δ⁡(x+y)≤max⁡{δ⁡(x),δ⁡(y)}\delta(x+y)\leq\max\{\delta(x),\delta(y)\}. Moreover, δ⁡(t)=1\delta(t)=1 and δ⁡(q)=0\delta(q)=0 for q∈ℚ×q\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}.

The associated valuation ring and maximal ideal are 𝒪={x:δ⁡(x)≤0}\mathcal{O}=\{x:\delta(x)\leq 0\} and 𝔪={x:δ⁡(x)<0}\mathfrak{m}=\{x:\delta(x)<0\}. Write k=𝒪/𝔪k=\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m} and res:𝒪→k\operatorname{res}:\mathcal{O}\to k for the residue map. Its restriction to ℚ\mathbb{Q} is injective. For n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, put Dn={x∈K:δ⁡(x)≤n}D_{n}=\{x\in K:\delta(x)\leq n\} and ℓn​(x)=res⁡(x/tn)\ell_{n}(x)=\operatorname{res}(x/t^{n}). This is a well-defined ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear map on DnD_{n}, with ℓn​(x)=0\ell_{n}(x)=0 exactly when δ⁡(x)<n\delta(x)<n, and ℓn​(tn)=1\ell_{n}(t^{n})=1. It also satisfies ℓr+s​(x​y)=ℓr​(x)​ℓs​(y)\ell_{r+s}(xy)=\ell_{r}(x)\ell_{s}(y) for x∈Drx\in D_{r}, y∈Dsy\in D_{s}. These identities supply the normalized functionals for the finite basis extensions.

2.4 Nonprincipal ultrafilters and ultrapowers

An ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} on ℕ\mathbb{N} is a proper filter such that, for every A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N}, exactly one of AA and ℕ∖A\mathbb{N}\setminus A belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Here a proper filter contains ℕ\mathbb{N}, excludes ∅\varnothing, and is closed under finite intersections and passage to supersets. It is nonprincipal if it contains no finite set. Such ultrafilters exist by extending the cofinite filter using Zorn’s lemma. Define (xn)∼(yn)(x_{n})\sim(y_{n}) when {n:xn=yn}∈𝒰\{n:x_{n}=y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}, and write E=Kℕ/𝒰E=K^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U} for the resulting ultrapower.

Addition and multiplication descend coordinatewise, making EE a field. If KK is algebraically closed, so is EE: roots of coordinate polynomials give a root in the quotient. A compatible lattice order on KK induces one on EE by [(xn)]≤E[(yn)][(x_{n})]\leq_{E}[(y_{n})] if {n:xn≤Kyn}∈𝒰\{n:x_{n}\leq_{K}y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}. Joins and meets are computed coordinatewise. The diagonal map j⁡(a)=[(a,a,…)]j(a)=[(a,a,\ldots)] is a field embedding preserving and reflecting order and preserving the lattice operations. These are instances of the ultraproduct preservation principle [13]. For countably infinite KK and nonprincipal 𝒰\mathcal{U} on ℕ\mathbb{N}, one has |E|=𝔠|E|=\mathfrak{c}.

2.5 Transcendence bases and extension of field embeddings

A set T⊆LT\subseteq L is algebraically independent over a subfield k0k_{0} if no nonzero polynomial over k0k_{0} in finitely many distinct elements of TT vanishes. A maximal such set is a transcendence basis; then L/k0​(T)L/k_{0}(T) is algebraic, and |T|=trdegk0⁡L|T|=\operatorname{trdeg}_{k_{0}}L. If k0k_{0} is countable and LL is uncountable, then |L|=trdegk0⁡L|L|=\operatorname{trdeg}_{k_{0}}L. Indeed, rational functions involve finitely many variables, and algebraic extensions add at most finitely many roots for each polynomial.

We also use the embedding-extension theorem: if L/DL/D is algebraic, Ω\Omega is algebraically closed, and σ:D↪Ω\sigma:D\hookrightarrow\Omega is a field embedding, then σ\sigma extends to an embedding L↪ΩL\hookrightarrow\Omega. It follows that algebraically closed extensions of a fixed field with equally sized transcendence bases are isomorphic over that field. Here, matching transcendence bases over KK and extending the induced rational-function-field isomorphism gives Φ:E→ℂ\Phi:E\to\mathbb{C} with Φ⁡(j⁡(a))=a\Phi(j(a))=a for a∈Ka\in K. Surjectivity follows because the image is algebraically closed and ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraic over it. Transporting the order through Φ\Phi preserves both field compatibility and the prescribed lattice identities on KK.

3 Conventions and finite positive basis extensions

All rings are commutative and have an identity. The symbols ≤\leq and ≥\geq on rational coefficients denote the usual order of ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Lemma 3.1.

Let P⊆RP\subseteq R satisfy

(1) 0∈P0\in P;

(2) P+P⊆PP+P\subseteq P;

(3) P∩(−P)={0}P\cap(-P)=\{0\};

(4) P​P⊆PPP\subseteq P.

Then ⪯\preceq is a partial order on PP, where ⪯\preceq is given by x⪯yx\preceq y if and only if y−x∈Py-x\in P.

Proof.

It is straightforward by checking all requirements. ∎

Given a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linearly independent set BB, write

PB=Coneℚ(B)={∑b∈Bqbb∣qb∈ℚ≥0,supp(q) finite},P_{B}=\operatorname{Cone}_{\mathbb{Q}}(B)=\{\sum_{b\in B}q_{b}b\mid q_{b}\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0},\ \operatorname{supp}(q)\text{ finite}\},

where supp⁡(q)={qb∈ℚ∣qb≠0}\operatorname{supp}(q)=\{q_{b}\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q_{b}\neq 0\} and ℚ≥0\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0} is the set of all nonnegative rational numbers.

Lemma 3.2.

([4]) Let VV be a subspace of a vector space WW. If BB is a basis of VV and the set {b1+V,⋯,bn+V}\{b_{1}+V,\cdot\cdot\cdot,b_{n}+V\} is a basis of W/VW/V, then B∪{b1,⋯,bn}B\cup\{b_{1},\cdot\cdot\cdot,b_{n}\} is a basis of WW.

Lemma 3.3.

Let BB be a basis of a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space VV and FF a nonempty finite subset of a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space EE containing VV. Put

Every totally ordered abelian group is torsion-free.

We now establish the coordinate characterization of the order. Let x=∑b∈Bxb​bx=\sum_{b\in B}x_{b}b and y=∑b∈Byb​by=\sum_{b\in B}y_{b}b. Then y−x=∑b∈B(yb−xb)​by-x=\sum_{b\in B}(y_{b}-x_{b})b. By uniqueness of the BB-expansion and the coordinate description of PP,

7 An algebraically closed ultrapower of cardinality continuum

Lemma 7.1.

There exists a nonprincipal ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} on ℕ\mathbb{N} containing every cofinite subset of ℕ\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

The cofinite subsets form a proper filter. The union of a chain of proper filters containing this filter is again a proper filter. Zorn’s lemma gives a maximal proper extension 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

If A∉𝒰A\notin\mathcal{U} and every F∈𝒰F\in\mathcal{U} met AA, adjoining AA would generate a proper larger filter. Thus some F∈𝒰F\in\mathcal{U} satisfies F∩A=∅F\cap A=\varnothing, and upward closure gives

ℕ∖A∈𝒰.\mathbb{N}\setminus A\in\mathcal{U}.

Therefore 𝒰\mathcal{U} is an ultrafilter. It contains no finite set, because the complement of any finite set already belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. ∎

Fix such an ultrafilter. On KℕK^{\mathbb{N}} define

(xn)∼(yn)⟺{n:xn=yn}∈𝒰,(x_{n})\sim(y_{n})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{n:x_{n}=y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U},

and set

E=Kℕ/𝒰.E=K^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U}.

An equivalence class is denoted by [(xn)][(x_{n})].

Proposition 7.2.

Coordinatewise addition and multiplication make EE an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. The map

j:K⟶E,j⁡(a)=[(a,a,…)]j:K\longrightarrow E,\qquad j(a)=[(a,a,\ldots)]

is an injective field homomorphism.

Proof.

Fix the ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} supplied by Lemma 7.1. Recall that ℕ∈𝒰\mathbb{N}\in\mathcal{U}, ∅∉𝒰\varnothing\notin\mathcal{U}, and 𝒰\mathcal{U} is closed under finite intersections and passage to supersets. We also use the ultrafilter property that, for every A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb{N}, exactly one of AA and ℕ∖A\mathbb{N}\setminus A belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

We first verify that the relation ∼\sim is an equivalence relation on KℕK^{\mathbb{N}}. For every sequence (xn)(x_{n}), the equality set {n∈ℕ:xn=xn}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:x_{n}=x_{n}\} is ℕ\mathbb{N}, which belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Thus (xn)∼(xn)(x_{n})\sim(x_{n}), proving reflexivity. Symmetry follows because {n:xn=yn}={n:yn=xn}\{n:x_{n}=y_{n}\}=\{n:y_{n}=x_{n}\}.

To prove transitivity, suppose that (xn)∼(yn)(x_{n})\sim(y_{n}) and (yn)∼(zn)(y_{n})\sim(z_{n}). Then A={n:xn=yn}∈𝒰A=\{n:x_{n}=y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U} and B={n:yn=zn}∈𝒰B=\{n:y_{n}=z_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}. Closure under finite intersections gives A∩B∈𝒰A\cap B\in\mathcal{U}. For every n∈A∩Bn\in A\cap B, we have xn=znx_{n}=z_{n}, so A∩B⊆{n:xn=zn}A\cap B\subseteq\{n:x_{n}=z_{n}\}. By upward closure, {n:xn=zn}∈𝒰\{n:x_{n}=z_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}. Hence (xn)∼(zn)(x_{n})\sim(z_{n}), proving transitivity.

Consequently, the quotient set E=Kℕ/𝒰E=K^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U} is well defined. We denote the equivalence class of (xn)(x_{n}) by [(xn)][(x_{n})].

Define addition and multiplication on EE by [(xn)]+[(yn)]=[(xn+yn)][(x_{n})]+[(y_{n})]=[(x_{n}+y_{n})] and [(xn)]​[(yn)]=[(xn​yn)][(x_{n})][(y_{n})]=[(x_{n}y_{n})]. We check that these definitions are independent of the representatives.

Suppose that (xn)∼(xn′)(x_{n})\sim(x^{\prime}_{n}) and (yn)∼(yn′)(y_{n})\sim(y^{\prime}_{n}). Then the sets A={n:xn=xn′}A=\{n:x_{n}=x^{\prime}_{n}\} and B={n:yn=yn′}B=\{n:y_{n}=y^{\prime}_{n}\} belong to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Therefore A∩B∈𝒰A\cap B\in\mathcal{U}. For every n∈A∩Bn\in A\cap B, we have both xn+yn=xn′+yn′x_{n}+y_{n}=x^{\prime}_{n}+y^{\prime}_{n} and xn​yn=xn′​yn′x_{n}y_{n}=x^{\prime}_{n}y^{\prime}_{n}. Thus the equality sets for the sum sequences and the product sequences both contain A∩BA\cap B. By upward closure, both equality sets belong to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. This proves (xn+yn)∼(xn′+yn′)(x_{n}+y_{n})\sim(x^{\prime}_{n}+y^{\prime}_{n}) and (xn​yn)∼(xn′​yn′)(x_{n}y_{n})\sim(x^{\prime}_{n}y^{\prime}_{n}). Hence addition and multiplication are well defined on EE.

Similarly, additive inverses are given by −[(xn)]=[(−xn)]-[(x_{n})]=[(-x_{n})]. Indeed, equivalent sequences have equivalent coordinatewise negatives.

Set 0E=[(0,0,…)]0_{E}=[(0,0,\ldots)] and 1E=[(1,1,…)]1_{E}=[(1,1,\ldots)]. The ring identities follow from the corresponding identities in KK, applied at every coordinate. For example, if X=[(xn)]X=[(x_{n})], Y=[(yn)]Y=[(y_{n})], and Z=[(zn)]Z=[(z_{n})], then

(X+Y)+Z=[((xn+yn)+zn)]=[(xn+(yn+zn))]=X+(Y+Z).(X+Y)+Z=[((x_{n}+y_{n})+z_{n})]=[(x_{n}+(y_{n}+z_{n}))]=X+(Y+Z).

Likewise,

X⁡(Y+Z)=[(xn​(yn+zn))]=[(xn​yn+xn​zn)]=X​Y+X​Z.X(Y+Z)=[(x_{n}(y_{n}+z_{n}))]=[(x_{n}y_{n}+x_{n}z_{n})]=XY+XZ.

Associativity of multiplication and commutativity of both operations follow in the same way. Moreover, X+0E=XX+0_{E}=X, X+(−X)=0EX+(-X)=0_{E}, and X​1E=XX1_{E}=X. Thus EE is a commutative ring with identity.

The identity and zero elements are distinct. Since 0≠10\neq 1 in KK, the equality set of the constant zero and constant one sequences is empty. As ∅∉𝒰\varnothing\notin\mathcal{U}, these sequences are not equivalent. Therefore 0E≠1E0_{E}\neq 1_{E}.

We now prove that every nonzero element of EE is invertible. Let X=[(xn)]≠0EX=[(x_{n})]\neq 0_{E}. By the definition of the equivalence relation, X=0E⇔{n:xn=0}∈𝒰X=0_{E}\iff\{n:x_{n}=0\}\in\mathcal{U}. Since X≠0EX\neq 0_{E}, the set {n:xn=0}\{n:x_{n}=0\} does not belong to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. The ultrafilter property therefore implies that its complement A={n:xn≠0}A=\{n:x_{n}\neq 0\} belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

Define a sequence (yn)(y_{n}) by yn={xn−1,n∈A,0,n∉A.y_{n}=\begin{cases}x_{n}^{-1},&n\in A,\\ 0,&n\notin A.\end{cases} The inverse xn−1x_{n}^{-1} exists whenever n∈An\in A, because KK is a field. Put Y=[(yn)]Y=[(y_{n})]. For every n∈An\in A, we have xn​yn=1x_{n}y_{n}=1. Hence A⊆{n:xn​yn=1}A\subseteq\{n:x_{n}y_{n}=1\}. By upward closure, the latter set belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Thus (xn​yn)∼(1,1,…)(x_{n}y_{n})\sim(1,1,\ldots), and consequently X​Y=[(xn​yn)]=1EXY=[(x_{n}y_{n})]=1_{E}. Since multiplication is commutative, we also have Y​X=1EYX=1_{E}. Therefore every nonzero element of EE has a multiplicative inverse, and EE is a field.

Consider the map j:K→E,j⁡(a)=[(a,a,…)]j:K\to E,\qquad j(a)=[(a,a,\ldots)]. Coordinatewise addition and multiplication give j⁡(a+b)=j⁡(a)+j⁡(b)j(a+b)=j(a)+j(b) and j⁡(a​b)=j⁡(a)​j​(b)j(ab)=j(a)j(b) for every a,b∈Ka,b\in K. Also, j⁡(0)=0Ej(0)=0_{E} and j⁡(1)=1Ej(1)=1_{E}, so jj is a unital ring homomorphism.

To prove injectivity, let a,b∈Ka,b\in K. If a=ba=b, the equality set of their constant sequences is ℕ\mathbb{N}, so j⁡(a)=j⁡(b)j(a)=j(b). If a≠ba\neq b, that equality set is empty, so j⁡(a)≠j⁡(b)j(a)\neq j(b). Hence j⁡(a)=j⁡(b)⇔a=bj(a)=j(b)\iff a=b. Thus jj is injective. Since KK and EE are fields, it follows that jj is a field embedding. Explicitly, for a≠0a\neq 0, the identity j⁡(a)​j​(a−1)=j⁡(1)=1Ej(a)j(a^{-1})=j(1)=1_{E} shows that j⁡(a−1)=j​(a)−1j(a^{-1})=j(a)^{-1}.

The field EE has characteristic zero. Indeed, for every positive integer mm, we have m​1E=j⁡(m​1K)m1_{E}=j(m1_{K}). Since KK has characteristic zero, m​1K≠0m1_{K}\neq 0. Injectivity of jj therefore gives m​1E≠0m1_{E}\neq 0. Thus no positive integer annihilates 1E1_{E}, which proves char⁡(E)=0\operatorname{char}(E)=0.

It remains to prove that EE is algebraically closed. Let

f⁡(T)=ad​Td+ad−1​Td−1+⋯+a0∈E⁡[T]f(T)=a_{d}T^{d}+a_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0}\in E[T]

be a nonconstant polynomial, where d≥1d\geq 1 and ad≠0Ea_{d}\neq 0_{E}.

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, define the coordinate polynomial

fn​(T)=ad,n​Td+ad−1,n​Td−1+⋯+a0,n∈K⁡[T].f_{n}(T)=a_{d,n}T^{d}+a_{d-1,n}T^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0,n}\in K[T].

If n∈Adn\in A_{d}, then ad,n≠0a_{d,n}\neq 0, so fnf_{n} has degree exactly dd. In particular, it is nonconstant. Since KK is algebraically closed, fnf_{n} has a root in KK.

For each n∈Adn\in A_{d}, choose rn∈Kr_{n}\in K such that fn​(rn)=0f_{n}(r_{n})=0. These choices can be made explicitly using the countability of KK: fix an enumeration K={c1,c2,…}K=\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots\} and choose rnr_{n} to be the first element of this enumeration that is a root of fnf_{n}. For n∉Adn\notin A_{d}, put rn=0r_{n}=0. This defines a sequence (rn)∈Kℕ(r_{n})\in K^{\mathbb{N}}. Set R=[(rn)]∈ER=[(r_{n})]\in E.

Because addition and multiplication in EE are defined coordinatewise, polynomial evaluation satisfies f⁡(R)=[(fn​(rn))]f(R)=[(f_{n}(r_{n}))]. We have proved that every nonconstant polynomial over EE has a root in EE. Since EE is a field, the factor theorem then allows us to remove a linear factor and repeat the argument. Induction on the degree shows that every nonconstant polynomial over EE splits into linear factors over EE. Hence EE is algebraically closed. ∎

Proposition 7.3.

Define

[(xn)]≤E[(yn)]⟺{n:xn≤Kyn}∈𝒰.[(x_{n})]\leq_{E}[(y_{n})]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{n:x_{n}\leq_{K}y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}.

∨E[(yn)]\displaystyle\vee_{E}[(y_{n})] =[(xn∨Kyn)],\displaystyle=[(x_{n}\vee_{K}y_{n})],
[(xn)]∧E[(yn)]\displaystyle[(x_{n})]\wedge_{E}[(y_{n})] =[(xn∧Kyn)].\displaystyle=[(x_{n}\wedge_{K}y_{n})].

Hence AX≤EAYAX\leq_{E}AY. Since EE is commutative, multiplication on the right by a nonnegative element also preserves order.

Moreover, 0≤K10\leq_{K}1 at every coordinate, so {n:0≤K1}=ℕ∈𝒰\{n:0\leq_{K}1\}=\mathbb{N}\in\mathcal{U}. Thus 0E≤E1E0_{E}\leq_{E}1_{E}. Proposition 7.2 gives 0E≠1E0_{E}\neq 1_{E}, and consequently 0E<E1E0_{E}<_{E}1_{E}.

j(a)∨Ej(b)=[(a∨Kb,a∨Kb,…)]=j(a∨Kb).j(a)\vee_{E}j(b)=[(a\vee_{K}b,a\vee_{K}b,\ldots)]=j(a\vee_{K}b).

∎

Proposition 7.4.

The field EE has cardinality

|E|=𝔠=2ℵ0.|E|=\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_{0}}.
Proof.

We prove the two cardinal inequalities separately.

Since KK is countable, choose an injective map ι:K→ℕ\iota:K\to\mathbb{N}. To each sequence x=(xn)n≥1∈Kℕx=(x_{n})_{n\geq 1}\in K^{\mathbb{N}}, associate the set Gx={(n,ι⁡(xn)):n∈ℕ}⊆ℕ×ℕG_{x}=\{(n,\iota(x_{n})):n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}. The assignment x↦Gxx\mapsto G_{x} is injective. Indeed, if Gx=GyG_{x}=G_{y}, then for every nn the unique pair in this set having first coordinate nn has second coordinate both ι⁡(xn)\iota(x_{n}) and ι⁡(yn)\iota(y_{n}). Thus ι⁡(xn)=ι⁡(yn)\iota(x_{n})=\iota(y_{n}), and injectivity of ι\iota gives xn=ynx_{n}=y_{n} for every nn.

Consequently, |Kℕ|≤|𝒫⁡(ℕ×ℕ)|=2ℵ0|K^{\mathbb{N}}|\leq|\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})|=2^{\aleph_{0}}, where the equality follows from the countability of ℕ×ℕ\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}. Since the quotient map Kℕ→EK^{\mathbb{N}}\to E is surjective, we obtain |E|≤|Kℕ|≤2ℵ0|E|\leq|K^{\mathbb{N}}|\leq 2^{\aleph_{0}}.

For the reverse inequality, we construct an injection from the set of binary sequences into EE. First, recall that no finite subset of ℕ\mathbb{N} belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Indeed, if F⊆ℕF\subseteq\mathbb{N} is finite, then its complement ℕ∖F\mathbb{N}\setminus F is cofinite and hence belongs to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. If FF also belonged to 𝒰\mathcal{U}, closure under finite intersections would imply ∅=F∩(ℕ∖F)∈𝒰\varnothing=F\cap(\mathbb{N}\setminus F)\in\mathcal{U}, contradicting the fact that 𝒰\mathcal{U} is a proper filter.

Because KK has characteristic zero, the canonical map ℤ→K\mathbb{Z}\to K is injective. We therefore identify integers with their images in KK. In particular, a nonzero integer remains nonzero when regarded as an element of KK.

Let

ε=(εj)j≥1∈{0,1}ℕ.\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_{j})_{j\geq 1}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, define

an​(ε)=∑j=1nεj​2j−1∈ℤ⊆K.a_{n}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varepsilon_{j}2^{j-1}\in\mathbb{Z}\subseteq K.

Thus an​(ε)a_{n}(\varepsilon) encodes the first nn entries of ε\varepsilon as an integer. Define Φ:{0,1}ℕ→E\Phi:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to E by Φ⁡(ε)=[(an​(ε))n≥1]\Phi(\varepsilon)=[(a_{n}(\varepsilon))_{n\geq 1}].

We claim that Φ\Phi is injective. Let ε,η∈{0,1}ℕ\varepsilon,\eta\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} be distinct, and let

r=min⁡{j≥1:εj≠ηj}.r=\min\{j\geq 1:\varepsilon_{j}\neq\eta_{j}\}.

Such an index exists because the sequences are distinct and ℕ\mathbb{N} is well ordered.

For every n<rn<r, the first nn entries of the two sequences agree. Hence an​(ε)=an​(η)a_{n}(\varepsilon)=a_{n}(\eta).

Now fix n≥rn\geq r. Computing in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, we have

an​(ε)−an​(η)=(εr−ηr)​2r−1+∑j=r+1n(εj−ηj)​2j−1.a_{n}(\varepsilon)-a_{n}(\eta)=(\varepsilon_{r}-\eta_{r})2^{r-1}+\sum_{j=r+1}^{n}(\varepsilon_{j}-\eta_{j})2^{j-1}.

Every term in the final sum is divisible by 2r2^{r}. More explicitly, put Mn=∑j=r+1n(εj−ηj)​2j−r−1∈ℤM_{n}=\sum_{j=r+1}^{n}(\varepsilon_{j}-\eta_{j})2^{j-r-1}\in\mathbb{Z}, with the empty sum interpreted as zero when n=rn=r. Then an​(ε)−an​(η)=2r−1​((εr−ηr)+2​Mn)a_{n}(\varepsilon)-a_{n}(\eta)=2^{r-1}\bigl((\varepsilon_{r}-\eta_{r})+2M_{n}\bigr).

Since εr\varepsilon_{r} and ηr\eta_{r} are distinct binary digits, εr−ηr\varepsilon_{r}-\eta_{r} is either 11 or −1-1. Thus (εr−ηr)+2​Mn(\varepsilon_{r}-\eta_{r})+2M_{n} is an odd integer and cannot be zero. Therefore an​(ε)−an​(η)a_{n}(\varepsilon)-a_{n}(\eta) is a nonzero integer. By the characteristic-zero embedding ℤ↪K\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow K, it is also nonzero in KK. Consequently, an​(ε)≠an​(η)a_{n}(\varepsilon)\neq a_{n}(\eta) for every n≥rn\geq r.

It follows that the equality set of the two representing sequences is exactly {n∈ℕ:an​(ε)=an​(η)}={1,…,r−1}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:a_{n}(\varepsilon)=a_{n}(\eta)\}=\{1,\ldots,r-1\}, where the right-hand side is empty if r=1r=1. This set is finite, so it does not belong to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. By the definition of the equivalence relation used to form EE, the sequences (an​(ε))(a_{n}(\varepsilon)) and (an​(η))(a_{n}(\eta)) are therefore not equivalent. Hence Φ⁡(ε)≠Φ⁡(η)\Phi(\varepsilon)\neq\Phi(\eta), proving injectivity.

Finally, the set {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} has cardinality 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}. Indeed, the assignment ε↦{j∈ℕ:εj=1}\varepsilon\mapsto\{j\in\mathbb{N}:\varepsilon_{j}=1\} is a bijection from {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} onto 𝒫⁡(ℕ)\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}). The injection Φ\Phi consequently gives 2ℵ0≤|E|2^{\aleph_{0}}\leq|E|.

Combining this with the upper bound and applying the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem, we conclude that |E|=2ℵ0=𝔠|E|=2^{\aleph_{0}}=\mathfrak{c}. ∎

8 A field isomorphism fixing the countable subfield

Lemma 8.1.

Let LL be an uncountable extension of a countable field k0k_{0}, with |L|=κ|L|=\kappa. Then

trdegk0⁡L=κ.\operatorname{trdeg}_{k_{0}}L=\kappa.
Proof.

Let L/k0L/k_{0} be the given field extension, where k0k_{0} is countable and |L|=κ>ℵ0|L|=\kappa>\aleph_{0}. We first choose a transcendence basis and then estimate the cardinality of the resulting algebraic extension.

Consider the family 𝒜\mathcal{A} of all subsets of LL that are algebraically independent over k0k_{0}, ordered by inclusion. This family is nonempty because it contains the empty set. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a chain in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and put S=⋃A∈𝒞AS=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal{C}}A.

The set SS is algebraically independent over k0k_{0}. Indeed, any polynomial relation among elements of SS involves only finitely many of them. Since 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a chain, those finitely many elements all belong to a single member of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Algebraic independence of that member excludes every nonzero polynomial relation among them. Thus S∈𝒜S\in\mathcal{A}, and SS is an upper bound for the chain.

By Zorn’s lemma, there exists a maximal algebraically independent subset T⊆LT\subseteq L over k0k_{0}. Set F=k0​(T)F=k_{0}(T), the subfield of LL generated by k0k_{0} and TT.

We claim that LL is algebraic over FF. Suppose otherwise. Then there exists a∈La\in L that is transcendental over FF. We show that T∪{a}T\cup\{a\} is algebraically independent over k0k_{0}, contradicting the maximality of TT.

Suppose that a nonzero polynomial relation among finitely many distinct elements t1,…,ts∈Tt_{1},\ldots,t_{s}\in T and aa were to hold. Such a relation has the form P⁡(t1,…,ts,a)=0P(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s},a)=0, where P⁡(Y1,…,Ys,Z)∈k0​[Y1,…,Ys,Z]P(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{s},Z)\in k_{0}[Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{s},Z] is nonzero. Write

P⁡(Y1,…,Ys,Z)=∑j=0dPj​(Y1,…,Ys)​Zj.P(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{s},Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}P_{j}(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{s})Z^{j}.

At least one coefficient polynomial PjP_{j} is nonzero. Since TT is algebraically independent over k0k_{0}, every such nonzero coefficient polynomial satisfies Pj​(t1,…,ts)≠0P_{j}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})\neq 0. Therefore Q⁡(Z)=∑j=0dPj​(t1,…,ts)​ZjQ(Z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}P_{j}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{s})Z^{j} is a nonzero polynomial in F⁡[Z]F[Z]. But the assumed relation gives Q⁡(a)=0Q(a)=0, contradicting the transcendence of aa over FF. Hence T∪{a}T\cup\{a\} is algebraically independent, and the claim follows.

Thus TT is a transcendence basis of LL over k0k_{0}, so trdegk0⁡L=|T|\operatorname{trdeg}_{k_{0}}L=|T|. It remains to prove that |T|=κ|T|=\kappa.

Put μ=max⁡{ℵ0,|T|}\mu=\max\{\aleph_{0},|T|\}. This is an infinite cardinal, regardless of whether TT is finite or infinite. We first prove that |F|≤μ|F|\leq\mu.

Let k0​[T]k_{0}[T] denote the subring of LL generated by k0k_{0} and TT. Every element of this ring is a polynomial expression involving only finitely many elements of TT. Consequently, k0​[T]=⋃{k0​[S]:S⊆T​ is finite}k_{0}[T]=\bigcup\{k_{0}[S]:S\subseteq T\text{ is finite}\}.

The family of finite subsets of TT has cardinality at most μ\mu: each finite subset can be listed by a finite tuple of elements of TT, and the set of all such finite tuples has cardinality at most μ\mu.

For each finite subset S={s1,…,sr}⊆TS=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}\}\subseteq T, the ring k0​[S]k_{0}[S] is at most countable. Indeed, each of its elements is represented by a polynomial in finitely many variables over the countable field k0k_{0}. Such a polynomial is specified by a finite list of coefficients from k0k_{0} and exponent vectors from ℕ0r\mathbb{N}_{0}^{r}. Both sets are at most countable, so there are at most countably many such finite lists. Therefore |k0​[S]|≤ℵ0|k_{0}[S]|\leq\aleph_{0}.

Taking the union over all finite subsets S⊆TS\subseteq T, we obtain |k0​[T]|≤μ⋅ℵ0=μ|k_{0}[T]|\leq\mu\cdot\aleph_{0}=\mu.

The ring k0​[T]k_{0}[T] is an integral domain because it is a subring of the field LL, and its fraction field is F=k0​(T)F=k_{0}(T). Thus every element of FF can be written as p/qp/q, where p,q∈k0​[T]p,q\in k_{0}[T] and q≠0q\neq 0. The number of such pairs is at most μ2=μ\mu^{2}=\mu, so |F|≤μ|F|\leq\mu.

We next count the polynomials over FF. For every fixed d∈ℕ0d\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, a polynomial of degree at most dd is determined by its d+1d+1 coefficients. Hence the set of such polynomials has cardinality at most |F|d+1≤μ|F|^{d+1}\leq\mu. Every polynomial has finite degree, so taking a countable union gives |F⁡[X]|≤ℵ0⋅μ=μ|F[X]|\leq\aleph_{0}\cdot\mu=\mu.

For each nonzero polynomial f∈F⁡[X]f\in F[X], let ZL​(f)={a∈L:f⁡(a)=0}Z_{L}(f)=\{a\in L:f(a)=0\}. Since LL is a field, a nonzero polynomial of degree dd has at most dd distinct roots in LL. In particular, every set ZL​(f)Z_{L}(f) is finite. A nonzero constant polynomial has no roots, which causes no exception to this statement.

Because LL is algebraic over FF, every element of LL belongs to ZL​(f)Z_{L}(f) for some nonzero polynomial f∈F⁡[X]f\in F[X]. Therefore L=⋃f∈F⁡[X]∖{0}ZL​(f)L=\bigcup_{f\in F[X]\setminus\{0\}}Z_{L}(f). There are at most μ\mu polynomials in this union, and each root set is finite. Consequently, κ=|L|≤μ⋅ℵ0=μ=max⁡{ℵ0,|T|}\kappa=|L|\leq\mu\cdot\aleph_{0}=\mu=\max\{\aleph_{0},|T|\}.

On the other hand, T⊆LT\subseteq L gives |T|≤κ|T|\leq\kappa. If |T|≤ℵ0|T|\leq\aleph_{0}, the preceding estimate would imply κ≤ℵ0\kappa\leq\aleph_{0}, contrary to the assumption that LL is uncountable. Thus |T|>ℵ0|T|>\aleph_{0}, and hence μ=|T|\mu=|T|. We obtain κ≤|T|≤κ\kappa\leq|T|\leq\kappa, so |T|=κ|T|=\kappa.

Since TT is a transcendence basis, it follows that trdegk0⁡L=|T|=κ\operatorname{trdeg}_{k_{0}}L=|T|=\kappa. ∎

Lemma 8.2.

Let L/D0L/D_{0} be an algebraic field extension, let Ω\Omega be algebraically closed, and let σ0:D0→Ω\sigma_{0}:D_{0}\to\Omega be a field embedding. Then σ0\sigma_{0} extends to a field embedding L→ΩL\to\Omega.

Define σ∗:D∗→Ω\sigma_{*}:D_{*}\to\Omega by setting σ∗​(x)=σλ​(x)\sigma_{*}(x)=\sigma_{\lambda}(x) whenever x∈Dλx\in D_{\lambda}. This definition is independent of λ\lambda. To see this, suppose that x∈Dλ∩Dμx\in D_{\lambda}\cap D_{\mu}. Since the pairs form a chain, one extends the other, so their embeddings agree on the smaller domain and hence agree at xx.

For x,y∈D∗x,y\in D_{*}, choose a member of the chain containing both. Since its embedding preserves addition and multiplication, so does σ∗\sigma_{*}. Moreover, σ∗​(1)=1\sigma_{*}(1)=1. If σ∗​(x)=0\sigma_{*}(x)=0, choose DλD_{\lambda} containing xx. Then σλ​(x)=0\sigma_{\lambda}(x)=0, and injectivity of σλ\sigma_{\lambda} gives x=0x=0. Thus σ∗\sigma_{*} is a field embedding. It extends every σλ\sigma_{\lambda} and agrees with σ0\sigma_{0} on D0D_{0}. Therefore (D∗,σ∗)(D_{*},\sigma_{*}) is an upper bound for the chain. The empty chain has the upper bound (D0,σ0)(D_{0},\sigma_{0}).

By Zorn’s lemma, 𝒫\mathcal{P} has a maximal element, which we denote by (D,σ)(D,\sigma). We prove that D=LD=L.

The embedding σ\sigma is an isomorphism from DD onto its image σ⁡(D)\sigma(D). Proposition 8.3.

There exists a field isomorphism

Φ:E⟶ℂ\Phi:E\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}

such that

Φ⁡(j⁡(a))=a(a∈K).\Phi(j(a))=a\qquad(a\in K).
Proof.

We retain the distinction between K⊆ℂK\subseteq\mathbb{C} and its diagonal image j⁡(K)⊆Ej(K)\subseteq E. Put F=j⁡(K)F=j(K). Since j:K→Ej:K\to E is an injective field homomorphism, the map η:F→K,η⁡(j⁡(a))=a\eta:F\to K,\qquad\eta(j(a))=a is a well-defined field isomorphism.

By Proposition 7.2, the field EE is algebraically closed, and by Proposition 7.4 it has cardinality 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. The field ℂ\mathbb{C} is also algebraically closed and has cardinality 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. Since KK is countable and jj is injective, both KK and F=j⁡(K)F=j(K) are countable. Applying Lemma 8.1 to the extensions E/FE/F and ℂ/K\mathbb{C}/K, we obtain trdegF⁡E=𝔠\operatorname{trdeg}_{F}E=\mathfrak{c} and trdegK⁡ℂ=𝔠\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}\mathbb{C}=\mathfrak{c}.

Choose a transcendence basis T⊆ET\subseteq E of EE over FF, and a transcendence basis S⊆ℂS\subseteq\mathbb{C} of ℂ\mathbb{C} over KK. Thus TT is algebraically independent over FF and EE is algebraic over F⁡(T)F(T); similarly, SS is algebraically independent over KK and ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraic over K⁡(S)K(S). The equalities of transcendence degrees give |T|=|S|=𝔠|T|=|S|=\mathfrak{c}, so we may choose a bijection θ:T→S\theta:T\to S.

We first construct an isomorphism between the corresponding rational function fields. Let F⁡[T]F[T] denote the subring of EE generated by FF and TT, and let K⁡[S]K[S] denote the subring of ℂ\mathbb{C} generated by KK and SS.

Every element of F⁡[T]F[T] can be written as f⁡(t1,…,tr)f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r}) for some finite list of distinct elements t1,…,tr∈Tt_{1},\ldots,t_{r}\in T and some polynomial f∈F⁡[X1,…,Xr]f\in F[X_{1},\ldots,X_{r}]. Let fη∈K⁡[X1,…,Xr]f^{\eta}\in K[X_{1},\ldots,X_{r}] be the polynomial obtained by applying η\eta to every coefficient of ff. Define

ψ⁡(f⁡(t1,…,tr))=fη​(θ⁡(t1),…,θ⁡(tr)).\psi(f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r}))=f^{\eta}(\theta(t_{1}),\ldots,\theta(t_{r})).

We verify that this definition is independent of the chosen polynomial expression. Suppose that two expressions represent the same element of F⁡[T]F[T]. By adjoining any missing variables, both expressions can be written using a common finite list t1,…,trt_{1},\ldots,t_{r} from TT. Thus we may suppose that f⁡(t1,…,tr)=g⁡(t1,…,tr)f(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r})=g(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r}) for polynomials f,g∈F⁡[X1,…,Xr]f,g\in F[X_{1},\ldots,X_{r}]. Then (f−g)​(t1,…,tr)=0(f-g)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{r})=0. Algebraic independence of TT over FF implies that f−gf-g is the zero polynomial. Applying η\eta to its coefficients gives fη=gηf^{\eta}=g^{\eta}, and therefore the two prescribed images are equal. Hence ψ\psi is well defined.

Coefficient transport and substitution preserve addition and multiplication, so ψ\psi is a unital ring homomorphism. Applying the same construction with η−1\eta^{-1} and θ−1\theta^{-1} gives an inverse map from K⁡[S]K[S] to F⁡[T]F[T]. The algebraic independence of SS ensures that this inverse is well defined by the same argument. Consequently, ψ:F⁡[T]→K⁡[S]\psi:F[T]\to K[S] is a ring isomorphism satisfying ψ⁡(c)=η⁡(c)\psi(c)=\eta(c) for c∈Fc\in F and ψ⁡(t)=θ⁡(t)\psi(t)=\theta(t) for t∈Tt\in T.

The fraction fields of F⁡[T]F[T] and K⁡[S]K[S] are F⁡(T)F(T) and K⁡(S)K(S), respectively. Extend ψ\psi to a map ϕ0:F⁡(T)→K⁡(S)\phi_{0}:F(T)\to K(S) by defining ϕ0​(p/q)=ψ⁡(p)/ψ⁡(q)\phi_{0}(p/q)=\psi(p)/\psi(q) for p,q∈F⁡[T]p,q\in F[T] with q≠0q\neq 0.

The denominator is nonzero because ψ\psi is injective. To verify independence of the fraction representation, suppose that p/q=p′/q′p/q=p^{\prime}/q^{\prime} with q,q′≠0q,q^{\prime}\neq 0. Then p​q′=p′​qpq^{\prime}=p^{\prime}q in the integral domain F⁡[T]F[T]. Applying ψ\psi gives ψ⁡(p)​ψ​(q′)=ψ⁡(p′)​ψ​(q)\psi(p)\psi(q^{\prime})=\psi(p^{\prime})\psi(q), so the resulting fractions are equal. Thus ϕ0\phi_{0} is well defined. It preserves addition and multiplication by the usual rules for fractions, and the corresponding extension of ψ−1\psi^{-1} is its inverse. Therefore ϕ0\phi_{0} is a field isomorphism.

In particular, ϕ0\phi_{0} extends η\eta on FF and sends every t∈Tt\in T to θ⁡(t)\theta(t). Hence ϕ0​(j​(a))=a\phi_{0}(j(a))=a for every a∈Ka\in K.

Since E/F⁡(T)E/F(T) is algebraic and ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraically closed, Lemma 8.2 applies to the embedding ϕ0:F⁡(T)→ℂ\phi_{0}:F(T)\to\mathbb{C}. It gives a field embedding Φ:E→ℂ\Phi:E\to\mathbb{C} such that Φ|F⁡(T)=ϕ0\Phi|_{F(T)}=\phi_{0}.

It remains to prove that Φ\Phi is surjective. Let M=Φ⁡(E)M=\Phi(E), which is a subfield of ℂ\mathbb{C}. Since Φ\Phi extends ϕ0\phi_{0} and ϕ0​(F⁡(T))=K⁡(S)\phi_{0}(F(T))=K(S), we have K⁡(S)⊆M⊆ℂK(S)\subseteq M\subseteq\mathbb{C}.

We first show that MM is algebraically closed. Let h⁡(X)=cd​Xd+⋯+c0∈M⁡[X]h(X)=c_{d}X^{d}+\cdots+c_{0}\in M[X] be nonconstant, with d≥1d\geq 1 and cd≠0c_{d}\neq 0. For each coefficient, choose its preimage ar∈Ea_{r}\in E under Φ\Phi, so Φ⁡(ar)=cr\Phi(a_{r})=c_{r}. Since Φ\Phi is injective, ad≠0a_{d}\neq 0. Thus g⁡(X)=ad​Xd+⋯+a0∈E⁡[X]g(X)=a_{d}X^{d}+\cdots+a_{0}\in E[X] is nonconstant.

Because EE is algebraically closed, there exists u∈Eu\in E such that g⁡(u)=0g(u)=0. Applying Φ\Phi yields h⁡(Φ⁡(u))=Φ⁡(g⁡(u))=0h(\Phi(u))=\Phi(g(u))=0. The element Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u) belongs to MM, so every nonconstant polynomial over MM has a root in MM. Hence MM is algebraically closed.

Next, ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraic over MM. Indeed, ℂ\mathbb{C} is algebraic over K⁡(S)K(S) because SS is a transcendence basis. For any z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, there is therefore a nonzero polynomial f∈K​(S)​[X]f\in K(S)[X] with f⁡(z)=0f(z)=0. Since K⁡(S)⊆MK(S)\subseteq M, the same polynomial belongs to M⁡[X]M[X] and remains nonzero. Thus zz is algebraic over MM.

An algebraically closed field has no proper algebraic field extension. To apply this fact explicitly, fix z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} and let mz​(X)∈M​[X]m_{z}(X)\in M[X] be its monic minimal polynomial over MM. This polynomial is irreducible and has positive degree. Since MM is algebraically closed, it has a root w∈Mw\in M. The factor theorem gives X−wX-w as a factor of mzm_{z}. Irreducibility therefore forces mz​(X)=X−wm_{z}(X)=X-w. Evaluating at zz gives z=w∈Mz=w\in M.

Thus every element of ℂ\mathbb{C} belongs to MM, so Φ⁡(E)=M=ℂ\Phi(E)=M=\mathbb{C}. Therefore Φ\Phi is a field isomorphism.

Finally, for every a∈Ka\in K, we have j⁡(a)∈F⊆F⁡(T)j(a)\in F\subseteq F(T), and hence Φ⁡(j⁡(a))=ϕ0​(j⁡(a))=η⁡(j⁡(a))=a\Phi(j(a))=\phi_{0}(j(a))=\eta(j(a))=a. Thus the isomorphism has the required restriction to the diagonal copy of KK. ∎

9 The lattice order on the usual complex field

Theorem 9.1.

Let t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} satisfy t>1t>1 and be transcendental over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. There exists a partial order ⪯\preceq on the usual complex field such that

z⪯w\displaystyle z\preceq w ⟹z+a⪯w+a\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ z+a\preceq w+a (z,w,a∈ℂ),\displaystyle(z,w,a\in\mathbb{C}),
0⪯z, 0⪯w\displaystyle 0\preceq z,\ 0\preceq w ⟹ 0⪯z​w\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ 0\preceq zw (z,w∈ℂ),\displaystyle(z,w\in\mathbb{C}),

and every pair has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound. The order can be chosen so that

It restricts to the usual order on ℚ\mathbb{Q} and to the order ≤K\leq_{K} on the subfield KK constructed above.

Proof.

Fix a real number t>1t>1 that is transcendental over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Let K⊆ℂK\subseteq\mathbb{C} be the countable algebraically closed subfield constructed above, and choose the basis BB as in Theorem 5.1 and Proposition 6.2. In particular, KK contains ℚ\mathbb{Q}, tt, and ii.

Put PK=PBP_{K}=P_{B}, and let ≤K\leq_{K} be the compatible lattice order supplied by Proposition 6.1. Its restriction to ℚ\mathbb{Q} is the usual order, and Propositions 6.1 and 6.2 give 0<K10<_{K}1, 0∨Ki=t0\vee_{K}i=t, and 1∧Kt=01\wedge_{K}t=0.

Choose the ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} from Lemma 7.1, and let E=Kℕ/𝒰E=K^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U}. By Proposition 7.3, the field EE carries a compatible lattice order ≤E\leq_{E}, and the diagonal embedding j:K→E,j⁡(a)=[(a,a,…)]j:K\to E,\qquad j(a)=[(a,a,\ldots)] preserves and reflects order and preserves joins and meets.

By Proposition 8.3, there is a field isomorphism Φ:E→ℂ\Phi:E\to\mathbb{C} satisfying Φ⁡(j⁡(a))=a\Phi(j(a))=a for every a∈Ka\in K. Since Φ\Phi is bijective, this also gives Φ−1​(a)=j​(a)\Phi^{-1}(a)=j(a) for every a∈Ka\in K.

Let PE={X∈E:0E≤EX}P_{E}=\{X\in E:0_{E}\leq_{E}X\} be the nonnegative cone of EE. Explicitly, PE={[(xn)]∈E:{n:xn∈PK}∈𝒰}P_{E}=\{[(x_{n})]\in E:\{n:x_{n}\in P_{K}\}\in\mathcal{U}\}. This description is independent of representatives by Proposition 7.3.

Define Pℂ=Φ⁡(PE)P_{\mathbb{C}}=\Phi(P_{E}) and define a relation ⪯\preceq on ℂ\mathbb{C} by z⪯w⇔w−z∈Pℂz\preceq w\iff w-z\in P_{\mathbb{C}}. All additions and multiplications on ℂ\mathbb{C} appearing below are its usual field operations.

The relation can equivalently be described by transporting the order on EE through Φ\Phi. Indeed, because Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is a field homomorphism, Φ−1​(w−z)=Φ−1​(w)−Φ−1​(z)\Phi^{-1}(w-z)=\Phi^{-1}(w)-\Phi^{-1}(z). Consequently, z⪯w⇔Φ−1(w−z)∈PE⇔Φ−1(z)≤EΦ−1(w)z\preceq w\iff\Phi^{-1}(w-z)\in P_{E}\iff\Phi^{-1}(z)\leq_{E}\Phi^{-1}(w).

If both zz and −z-z belong to PℂP_{\mathbb{C}}, then X=Φ−1​(z)X=\Phi^{-1}(z) and −X=Φ−1​(−z)-X=\Phi^{-1}(-z) both belong to PEP_{E}. Hence X=0EX=0_{E}, so z=0z=0. Therefore Pℂ∩(−Pℂ)={0}P_{\mathbb{C}}\cap(-P_{\mathbb{C}})=\{0\}.

If z,w∈Pℂz,w\in P_{\mathbb{C}}, write again z=Φ⁡(X)z=\Phi(X) and w=Φ⁡(Y)w=\Phi(Y) with X,Y∈PEX,Y\in P_{E}. Since X​Y∈PEXY\in P_{E} and Φ\Phi preserves multiplication, z​w=Φ⁡(X)​Φ​(Y)=Φ⁡(X​Y)∈Pℂzw=\Phi(X)\Phi(Y)=\Phi(XY)\in P_{\mathbb{C}}. Thus Pℂ​Pℂ⊆PℂP_{\mathbb{C}}P_{\mathbb{C}}\subseteq P_{\mathbb{C}}.

We now check that ⪯\preceq is a partial order. For every z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, we have z−z=0∈Pℂz-z=0\in P_{\mathbb{C}}, so z⪯zz\preceq z. If z⪯wz\preceq w and w⪯zw\preceq z, then both w−zw-z and z−w=−(w−z)z-w=-(w-z) belong to PℂP_{\mathbb{C}}. The intersection property implies w−z=0w-z=0, so z=wz=w. Finally, if z⪯wz\preceq w and w⪯uw\preceq u, then u−z=(u−w)+(w−z)∈Pℂu-z=(u-w)+(w-z)\in P_{\mathbb{C}}, and hence z⪯uz\preceq u. This proves reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity.

The order is translation invariant. For any z,w,a∈ℂz,w,a\in\mathbb{C}, the identity (w+a)−(z+a)=w−z(w+a)-(z+a)=w-z gives z⪯w⇔z+a⪯w+az\preceq w\iff z+a\preceq w+a.

It is also compatible with multiplication. If 0⪯z0\preceq z and 0⪯w0\preceq w, then z,w∈Pℂz,w\in P_{\mathbb{C}}, so the multiplicative closure of this cone gives z​w∈Pℂzw\in P_{\mathbb{C}}. Equivalently, 0⪯z, 0⪯w⟹0⪯z​w0\preceq z,\ 0\preceq w\implies 0\preceq zw. More generally, if z⪯wz\preceq w and 0⪯a0\preceq a, then a​w−a​z=a⁡(w−z)∈Pℂaw-az=a(w-z)\in P_{\mathbb{C}}, so a​z⪯a​waz\preceq aw.

We next prove that every pair of complex numbers has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound. Let z,w∈ℂz,w\in\mathbb{C}, and put X=Φ−1​(z)X=\Phi^{-1}(z) and Y=Φ−1​(w)Y=\Phi^{-1}(w). Define u=Φ(X∨EY)u=\Phi(X\vee_{E}Y) and l=Φ(X∧EY)l=\Phi(X\wedge_{E}Y).

Since X≤EX∨EYX\leq_{E}X\vee_{E}Y and Y≤EX∨EYY\leq_{E}X\vee_{E}Y, the order-transport equivalence established above gives z⪯uz\preceq u and w⪯uw\preceq u. Thus uu is an upper bound of zz and ww.

Suppose that v∈ℂv\in\mathbb{C} is any other upper bound, so z⪯vz\preceq v and w⪯vw\preceq v. Transporting these inequalities to EE gives X≤EΦ−1(v)X\leq_{E}\Phi^{-1}(v) and Y≤EΦ−1(v)Y\leq_{E}\Phi^{-1}(v). By the least-upper-bound property in EE, X∨EY≤EΦ−1(v)X\vee_{E}Y\leq_{E}\Phi^{-1}(v). Transporting this inequality back to ℂ\mathbb{C} yields u⪯vu\preceq v. Therefore uu is the least upper bound, and z∨w=Φ(Φ−1(z)∨EΦ−1(w))z\vee w=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(z)\vee_{E}\Phi^{-1}(w)\bigr).

Similarly, X∧EY≤EXX\wedge_{E}Y\leq_{E}X and X∧EY≤EYX\wedge_{E}Y\leq_{E}Y imply l⪯zl\preceq z and l⪯wl\preceq w. If vv is any other lower bound of zz and ww, then Φ−1(v)≤EX\Phi^{-1}(v)\leq_{E}X and Φ−1(v)≤EY\Phi^{-1}(v)\leq_{E}Y. The greatest-lower-bound property in EE gives Φ−1(v)≤EX∧EY\Phi^{-1}(v)\leq_{E}X\wedge_{E}Y, and hence v⪯lv\preceq l. Thus ll is the greatest lower bound, and z∧w=Φ(Φ−1(z)∧EΦ−1(w))z\wedge w=\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(z)\wedge_{E}\Phi^{-1}(w)\bigr). Consequently, ⪯\preceq is a compatible lattice order on the usual complex field.

It remains to verify its restriction to KK and the specified identities. Let a,b∈Ka,b\in K. Since Φ−1​(a)=j​(a)\Phi^{-1}(a)=j(a) and Φ−1​(b)=j​(b)\Phi^{-1}(b)=j(b), we have a⪯b⇔j(a)≤Ej(b)⇔a≤Kba\preceq b\iff j(a)\leq_{E}j(b)\iff a\leq_{K}b, where the last equivalence uses the fact that jj preserves and reflects order. Thus the restriction of ⪯\preceq to KK is precisely ≤K\leq_{K}.

The lattice operations on KK are preserved as well. Since jj preserves joins,

a∨b=Φ(j(a)∨Ej(b))=Φ(j(a∨Kb))=a∨Kb.a\vee b=\Phi\bigl(j(a)\vee_{E}j(b)\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(j(a\vee_{K}b)\bigr)=a\vee_{K}b.

Likewise, preservation of meets gives

a∧b=Φ(j(a)∧Ej(b))=Φ(j(a∧Kb))=a∧Kb.a\wedge b=\Phi\bigl(j(a)\wedge_{E}j(b)\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(j(a\wedge_{K}b)\bigr)=a\wedge_{K}b.

In particular, for p,q∈ℚ⊆Kp,q\in\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K, we obtain p⪯q⇔p≤Kq⇔p≤qp\preceq q\iff p\leq_{K}q\iff p\leq q, where the final inequality is the usual rational order. Therefore ⪯\preceq restricts to the usual order on ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Write z≺wz\prec w when z⪯wz\preceq w and z≠wz\neq w. Since 0<K10<_{K}1 and the order on KK is preserved, we have 0⪯10\preceq 1. As 0≠10\neq 1 in ℂ\mathbb{C}, this gives 0≺10\prec 1. Finally, the identities from Proposition 6.2 transfer without change: 0∨i=0∨Ki=t0\vee i=0\vee_{K}i=t and 1∧t=1∧Kt=01\wedge t=1\wedge_{K}t=0. ∎

Proposition 9.2.

Fix the choices made in the construction. Given z,w∈ℂz,w\in\mathbb{C}, choose representatives

Φ−1​(z)=[(xn)],Φ−1​(w)=[(yn)],\Phi^{-1}(z)=[(x_{n})],\ \Phi^{-1}(w)=[(y_{n})],

and write their unique basis expansions

xn=∑b∈Bxn,bb,yn=∑b∈Byn,bb,xn,b,yn,b∈ℚ.x_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}x_{n,b}b,\ y_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}y_{n,b}b,x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\in\mathbb{Q}.

Then

z⪯w⟺{n∣∀b∈Bxn,b≤yn,b}∈𝒰.z\preceq w\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigl\{n\mid\forall b\in B\ x_{n,b}\leq y_{n,b}\bigr\}\in\mathcal{U}.

Moreover,

z∨w=Φ⁡[(∑b∈Bmax⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​b)n≥1]z\vee w=\Phi[(\sum_{b\in B}\max\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}\,b)_{n\geq 1}]

and

z∧w=Φ⁡[(∑b∈Bmin⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​b)n≥1]z\wedge w=\Phi[(\sum_{b\in B}\min\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}\,b)_{n\geq 1}]

Every sum is finite for each fixed nn; no uniform finite support across all nn is required.

Proof.

Fix the basis BB, the ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and the field isomorphism Φ:E→ℂ\Phi:E\to\mathbb{C} chosen in the preceding construction. Let z,w∈ℂz,w\in\mathbb{C}, and choose representatives such that X=Φ−1​(z)=[(xn)]X=\Phi^{-1}(z)=[(x_{n})] and Y=Φ−1​(w)=[(yn)]Y=\Phi^{-1}(w)=[(y_{n})].

For every n≥1n\geq 1, the basis property of BB gives unique expansions xn=∑b∈Bxn,b​bx_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}x_{n,b}b and yn=∑b∈Byn,b​by_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}y_{n,b}b, where xn,b,yn,b∈ℚx_{n,b},y_{n,b}\in\mathbb{Q} and only finitely many coefficients are nonzero. All comparisons, maxima, and minima of these coefficients are taken in the usual order on ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

For each nn, put Sn=suppB⁡(xn)∪suppB⁡(yn)S_{n}=\operatorname{supp}_{B}(x_{n})\cup\operatorname{supp}_{B}(y_{n}). This is a finite subset of BB. If b∉Snb\notin S_{n}, then xn,b=yn,b=0x_{n,b}=y_{n,b}=0.

We first establish the comparison formula. By Proposition 6.1, for every fixed nn, xn≤Kyn⇔xn,b≤yn,b for every b∈Bx_{n}\leq_{K}y_{n}\iff x_{n,b}\leq y_{n,b}\text{ for every }b\in B. Since both coefficients vanish outside SnS_{n}, the condition on the right can also be checked using only the finite set SnS_{n}.

It follows that the two subsets of ℕ\mathbb{N} {n:xn≤Kyn}\{n:x_{n}\leq_{K}y_{n}\} and C={n:(∀b∈B)​xn,b≤yn,b}C=\{n:(\forall b\in B)\ x_{n,b}\leq y_{n,b}\} are equal. The definition of the transported order on ℂ\mathbb{C} and Proposition 7.3 therefore give

z⪯w⇔X≤EY⇔{n:xn≤Kyn}∈𝒰⇔C∈𝒰.z\preceq w\iff X\leq_{E}Y\iff\{n:x_{n}\leq_{K}y_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}\iff C\in\mathcal{U}.

This is the asserted comparison formula. The universal condition over BB is evaluated at each fixed index nn when defining the set CC.

We next prove the formulas for joins and meets. For each n≥1n\geq 1, define un=∑b∈Bmax⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​bu_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}\max\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}b and vn=∑b∈Bmin⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​bv_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}\min\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}b. These expressions are well defined as elements of KK. Indeed, if b∉Snb\notin S_{n}, then both coefficients are zero, so their maximum and minimum are also zero. Thus suppB⁡(un)⊆Sn\operatorname{supp}_{B}(u_{n})\subseteq S_{n} and suppB⁡(vn)⊆Sn\operatorname{supp}_{B}(v_{n})\subseteq S_{n}. Both sums are consequently finite.

By the coordinate formulas in Proposition 6.1, we have un=xn∨Kynu_{n}=x_{n}\vee_{K}y_{n} and vn=xn∧Kynv_{n}=x_{n}\wedge_{K}y_{n} for every nn. Applying Proposition 7.3 to the representative sequences gives X∨EY=[(xn∨Kyn)]=[(un)]X\vee_{E}Y=[(x_{n}\vee_{K}y_{n})]=[(u_{n})] and X∧EY=[(xn∧Kyn)]=[(vn)]X\wedge_{E}Y=[(x_{n}\wedge_{K}y_{n})]=[(v_{n})].

The lattice operations on ℂ\mathbb{C} were defined by transport through Φ\Phi. Hence

z∨w=Φ(X∨EY)=Φ([(un)]),z\vee w=\Phi(X\vee_{E}Y)=\Phi([(u_{n})]),

which yields

z∨w=Φ⁡([(∑b∈Bmax⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​b)n≥1]).z\vee w=\Phi\left(\left[\left(\sum_{b\in B}\max\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}b\right)_{n\geq 1}\right]\right).

Likewise,

z∧w=Φ(X∧EY)=Φ([(vn)]),z\wedge w=\Phi(X\wedge_{E}Y)=\Phi([(v_{n})]),

and therefore

z∧w=Φ⁡([(∑b∈Bmin⁡{xn,b,yn,b}​b)n≥1]).z\wedge w=\Phi\left(\left[\left(\sum_{b\in B}\min\{x_{n,b},y_{n,b}\}b\right)_{n\geq 1}\right]\right).

We finally verify explicitly that all three formulas are independent of the representative sequences. Suppose that (xn′)(x^{\prime}_{n}) and (yn′)(y^{\prime}_{n}) are alternative representatives of XX and YY, respectively. Then Hx={n:xn=xn′}∈𝒰H_{x}=\{n:x_{n}=x^{\prime}_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U} and Hy={n:yn=yn′}∈𝒰H_{y}=\{n:y_{n}=y^{\prime}_{n}\}\in\mathcal{U}. Thus H=Hx∩Hy∈𝒰H=H_{x}\cap H_{y}\in\mathcal{U}.

Write the unique basis expansions of the new representatives as xn′=∑b∈Bxn,b′​bx^{\prime}_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}x^{\prime}_{n,b}b and yn′=∑b∈Byn,b′​by^{\prime}_{n}=\sum_{b\in B}y^{\prime}_{n,b}b. For every n∈Hn\in H, the equalities xn=xn′x_{n}=x^{\prime}_{n} and yn=yn′y_{n}=y^{\prime}_{n}, together with uniqueness of basis coordinates, imply xn,b=xn,b′x_{n,b}=x^{\prime}_{n,b} and yn,b=yn,b′y_{n,b}=y^{\prime}_{n,b} for every b∈Bb\in B simultaneously.

Let C′={n:(∀b∈B)​xn,b′≤yn,b′}C^{\prime}=\{n:(\forall b\in B)\ x^{\prime}_{n,b}\leq y^{\prime}_{n,b}\}. The preceding coordinate equalities show that C∩H=C′∩HC\cap H=C^{\prime}\cap H. If C∈𝒰C\in\mathcal{U}, then C∩H∈𝒰C\cap H\in\mathcal{U}, and the inclusion C∩H⊆C′C\cap H\subseteq C^{\prime} implies C′∈𝒰C^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}. The same argument with CC and C′C^{\prime} interchanged proves the converse. Therefore C∈𝒰⇔C′∈𝒰C\in\mathcal{U}\iff C^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}, so the comparison formula is independent of the representatives.

Define un′u^{\prime}_{n} and vn′v^{\prime}_{n} from the new coefficients by the same maximum and minimum formulas. For every n∈Hn\in H, equality of all corresponding coefficients gives un=un′u_{n}=u^{\prime}_{n} and vn=vn′v_{n}=v^{\prime}_{n}. Hence the equality sets {n:un=un′}\{n:u_{n}=u^{\prime}_{n}\} and {n:vn=vn′}\{n:v_{n}=v^{\prime}_{n}\} both contain HH and therefore belong to 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Consequently, [(un)]=[(un′)][(u_{n})]=[(u^{\prime}_{n})] and [(vn)]=[(vn′)][(v_{n})]=[(v^{\prime}_{n})]. Applying the fixed map Φ\Phi proves that the displayed join and meet formulas are also independent of representatives.

Throughout the argument, finiteness is required separately for each index nn. The finite set SnS_{n} may vary with nn: each unu_{n} and vnv_{n} is an element of KK, so the resulting sequences belong to KℕK^{\mathbb{N}}. No common finite support for all indices is needed. ∎
